newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko urges Belarus to back his referendum.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko urges Belarus to back his referendum.

text.p: Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, who flies to Moscow on Wednesday to promote closer ties with Russia, issued a direct appeal to voters to back him in his bid to boost his powers against a rebellious parliament.
"I seek your support," read the headline of a direct address published on Tuesday in Lukashenko's Sovyetskaya Byelorussiya newspaper as he asked for backing in a November 24 referendum.
The imposing, moustachioed leader, hand on heart and smiling, appeared in profile before a photograph of hundreds of people raising their hands in salute.

Copies of the newspaper, whose name means Soviet Byelorussia -- the name for Belarus before it split from the Soviet Union, a rift Lukashenko openly regrets -- were stuffed into letter-boxes across the capital.

Belarus usually publishes 200,000 copies of the daily, but on Tuesday, circulation rocketed to four million as Lukashenko published the draft constitution for which he is seeking approval at the referendum.
"I want to tell you honestly. We could continue living with the present constitution. But it will never bring peace and harmony to our common home," Lukashenko wrote.
Lukashenko, who will address the Russian parliament on Wednesday, enjoys widespread support for his anti-corruption stance and his policy of forming a union with Russia.

The deputy head of Lukashenko's administration, Vladimir Zametalin, told Reuters the president would propose a new integration plan to Russian deputies, a large proportion of whom are communists who share Lukashenko's goal of closer union.
He said the new union would be "no less radical" than the one which formed the Commonwealth of Independent States.
Russia and Belarus agreed to form a commonwealth earlier this year but Lukashenko has complained of slow progress since.

The head of the central electoral commission in Minsk, Viktor Gonchar, who has already declared he will not recognise the results of the referendum, is due to address the same session of Russia's State Duma or lower house.
"No one will be allowed to carry out anti-constitutional coups under cover of integration processes," he said.
Lukashenko is locked in a row with parliament which some analysts compare to a stalemate in Russia in 1993 which ended when President Boris Yeltsin sent tanks against parliament.
His opponents in the republic of 10 million sandwiched between Russia and Poland accuse him of building a dictatorship.
The West has also criticised Lukashenko, who regularly ignores the rulings of competing branches of power and issues decrees overturning their decisions.

Parliament and the constitutional court in Belarus have declared the results of the referendum will have no legal force, but Lukashenko overturned these rulings, though the present constitution does not give him the right to do this.
Lukashenko, 42, is seeking approval to restart his five-year term from the date of the vote, extending it by more than two years without elections.

His draft constitution would also create an upper house of parliament partly appointed by himself, and give him the right to appoint half the constitutional court, half the commission which monitors and organises elections and all court judges.
"Every branch of power will have only those powers which are essential for the defence of the interests of the individual and society," Lukashenko wrote.
"Then we will be able to sort out the inadequacies of the law and order bodies and defend our citizens from crime."
